blocks.content: NodePort solved external reachability but left every real production concern unaddressed: a single stable address, health aware routing, and no dependency on any one node staying alive. LoadBalancer is the cloud native answer to all three.
LoadBalancer, Given Its Own Full Depth
blocks.text: LoadBalancer, Given Its Own Full Depth

blocks.content: A LoadBalancer Service instructs Kubernetes to provision an actual external load balancer from the underlying cloud provider, such as an AWS Elastic Load Balancer, a GCP Load Balancer, or an Azure Load Balancer.

Setting a Service's type field to LoadBalancer is all that is required in the manifest. The cloud controller manager, introduced back in the Kubernetes Architecture module, detects the new Service and handles the actual provisioning automatically.

Once provisioned, the cloud load balancer receives its own genuinely public, stable IP address or DNS hostname, and any traffic sent to that address is distributed across every healthy node in the cluster.

This is the single most common way real production applications running on a managed cloud Kubernetes cluster expose themselves to the public internet, precisely because it requires no manual load balancer configuration at all.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/devops-content-images/1784641970150-650805519.png
blocks.alt: LoadBalancer given its own full depth

blocks.content: The Genuine Most Common Production Pattern
blocks.text: The Genuine Most Common Production Pattern

blocks.content: For teams running on a managed cloud provider, LoadBalancer is usually the very first Service type reached for once an application is ready to accept real external traffic, precisely because of how little manual work it requires.

The alternative of manually provisioning a cloud load balancer outside of Kubernetes, then manually pointing it at node IPs and NodePort values, is exactly the kind of tedious, error prone, manual process Kubernetes exists to eliminate.

By expressing the load balancer requirement declaratively, as a single line in a Service manifest, the same benefits of version control, code review, and repeatability that apply to every other Kubernetes object now apply to external exposure as well.
This declarative approach also means recreating the entire application, load balancer included, in a new cluster or a new region is often as simple as reapplying the same set of manifests.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/devops-content-images/1784641971882-829841438.png
blocks.alt: A cloud provisioned external load balancer

blocks.content: A Real LoadBalancer Example

Consider the same admin dashboard from the NodePort topic, now ready for real external users rather than just a handful of trusted engineers. Changing its Service type from NodePort to LoadBalancer is the entire required change.

Within a few minutes of applying that change, the cloud controller manager provisions an AWS Elastic Load Balancer automatically, and kubectl get svc admin-dashboard begins showing a genuine external IP address or hostname in its output.

Any client anywhere on the public internet can now reach the dashboard through that single, stable external address, with the cloud load balancer itself handling distribution across every healthy cluster node behind the scenes.

No manual load balancer console clicking, no manual target group configuration, and no manual health check setup was required. All of it was derived automatically from the single type field change in the manifest.

apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: admin-dashboard
spec:
  type: LoadBalancer
  selector:
    app: admin-dashboard
  ports:
    - port: 80
      targetPort: 8080

blocks.content: Recap: The Cloud Controller Manager

The Kubernetes Architecture module introduced the cloud controller manager as the component responsible for talking to a cloud provider's APIs on behalf of the cluster, handling things like nodes, storage volumes, and load balancers.

At the time, that description was necessarily brief, a single piece in a much larger architectural picture. This topic is the promised full depth treatment of exactly what the cloud controller manager does for Services specifically.

When a LoadBalancer Service is created, the cloud controller manager's Service controller watches for it, calls the appropriate cloud provider API to provision a real load balancer, and writes the resulting external address back onto the Service object.

This is a clean, concrete example of the controller pattern covered back in the Controller Manager topic: watch for a desired state, in this case a Service wanting a load balancer, and continuously reconcile the real world to match it.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/devops-content-images/1784641975634-730224406.png
blocks.alt: Recap of the cloud controller manager

blocks.content: Layering Three Service Types Together

A LoadBalancer Service does not replace NodePort or ClusterIP. It is built directly on top of both. Creating a LoadBalancer Service automatically allocates a NodePort as well, and that NodePort in turn sits on top of a ClusterIP.

The cloud load balancer's actual job is to receive external traffic and forward it to the cluster nodes on that automatically allocated NodePort, which then hands off to kube proxy exactly as already established in the previous topic.

This means every property already learned about ClusterIP and NodePort routing continues to apply, unchanged, underneath a LoadBalancer Service. LoadBalancer adds a genuinely external, stable entry point on top of everything already built.

Seeing this three layer stack clearly, ClusterIP at the bottom, NodePort in the middle, LoadBalancer at the top, is one of the most useful mental models for understanding Kubernetes Services as a whole.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/devops-content-images/1784641977336-677101397.png

A Common Mistake: One Load Balancer Per Service
blocks.text: A Common Mistake: One Load Balancer Per Service

blocks.content: A common and expensive mistake is creating a separate LoadBalancer Service for every single application component in a cluster, without considering that each one provisions its own real, billed cloud resource.

A cluster running twenty microservices, each with its own LoadBalancer Service, ends up with twenty separate cloud load balancers, each incurring its own hourly cost, even though most of those twenty components do not need public exposure at all.

In most real applications, only the handful of Services genuinely facing the public internet, typically just a frontend or a single API gateway, need to be type LoadBalancer. Everything else should remain ClusterIP.

For cases where multiple externally facing paths genuinely are needed behind a single address, an Ingress controller, covered later in this module, is almost always the more cost effective and more manageable solution than multiple LoadBalancers.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/devops-content-images/1784641979074-401728444.png
blocks.alt: The mistake of one load balancer per service

blocks.content: Cloud Provider Differences

The exact behavior of a LoadBalancer Service depends on which cloud provider the cluster runs on, since each cloud implements its own cloud controller manager plugin with provider specific defaults and annotations.
On AWS, a LoadBalancer Service typically provisions a Classic or Network Load Balancer by default, configurable to a specific type through provider specific annotations added to the Service manifest.

On GCP and Azure, the equivalent native load balancer products are provisioned instead, each with their own annotation based customization options for things like internal only load balancers or specific health check paths.

Running a cluster without any cloud provider integration, such as a bare metal or fully on premises cluster, means LoadBalancer Services will never be automatically provisioned unless a tool like MetalLB is installed to fill that gap.
Internal LoadBalancer Services

Not every LoadBalancer Service needs to be reachable from the public internet. Cloud providers support an internal load balancer variant, configured through a provider specific annotation, that is only reachable from within the same private network.

This internal variant is genuinely useful for exposing a Service to other systems that live outside the Kubernetes cluster but still inside the same private cloud network, such as a separate virtual machine fleet not yet migrated to Kubernetes.

It provides the same stable, real load balancer benefits already covered, health aware routing and a single stable address, without accepting any traffic whatsoever from the public internet, which is the correct choice for many internal integrations.

Recognizing when internal is the right choice, versus a genuinely public facing LoadBalancer, is an important part of correctly scoping exactly which systems should be able to reach a given application component.

kind: Service
metadata:
  name: internal-api
  annotations:
    service.beta.kubernetes.io/aws-load-balancer-internal: "true"
spec:
  type: LoadBalancer
  selector:
    app: internal-api
  ports:
    - port: 443
      targetPort: 8443

blocks.content: TLS Termination at the Load Balancer
blocks.text: TLS Termination at the Load Balancer

blocks.content: A cloud LoadBalancer Service can often be configured, through provider specific annotations, to terminate TLS encryption directly at the load balancer itself, decrypting HTTPS traffic before forwarding plain HTTP traffic on to the cluster.

This offloads the computational cost and certificate management complexity of TLS termination away from application Pods, letting application code focus purely on business logic rather than certificate handling.

Configuring this typically involves specifying a certificate reference in an annotation and adjusting the Service's port configuration to reflect the plain HTTP port the load balancer should forward decrypted traffic to internally.
This pattern is common enough in real production clusters that it is worth recognizing on sight, even though the exact annotation syntax differs meaningfully between AWS, GCP, and Azure.
LoadBalancer Failover Behavior

Cloud load balancers continuously perform their own health checks against the cluster nodes behind them, independent of Kubernetes's own readiness probe mechanism, and automatically stop routing traffic to any node that fails those checks.

This means a LoadBalancer Service provides a genuine extra layer of resilience beyond what NodePort alone offers: even a complete node failure is handled gracefully, with traffic automatically shifting to the remaining healthy nodes.

This external health checking happens in addition to, not instead of, the Pod level readiness checks already covered in earlier modules, giving a LoadBalancer Service two independent layers of health awareness working together.

Understanding this layered health checking helps explain why a LoadBalancer Service can continue serving traffic seamlessly through events that would otherwise cause a visible outage using a simpler, non load balanced access method.
Verifying a LoadBalancer Service in Practice
blocks.text: Verifying a LoadBalancer Service in Practice

blocks.content: Running kubectl get svc admin-dashboard immediately after creation typically shows the external IP column as pending, since real cloud provisioning takes a small amount of time to complete.
Watching with kubectl get svc admin-dashboard --watch shows that pending value transition to a real external IP address or hostname once the cloud provider finishes provisioning the load balancer.

A curl request from any machine on the public internet against that external address should now succeed, confirming both the cloud load balancer and the underlying NodePort and ClusterIP routing are all working correctly together.

If the external IP remains stuck on pending for an extended period, the most common cause is a cloud IAM permissions issue preventing the cloud controller manager from successfully calling the provider's load balancer provisioning API.
Cost and Operational Considerations

Every LoadBalancer Service is a genuinely billed cloud resource, typically charged per hour of existence plus data transfer, which makes the earlier warning about one load balancer per Service a real financial consideration, not just tidiness.

Teams running many small services in production commonly consolidate external exposure behind a small number of LoadBalancer Services fronting an Ingress controller, rather than provisioning one directly per application component.

Deleting a LoadBalancer Service also deletes the underlying cloud load balancer automatically, which is convenient for cleanup but also means accidental deletion of a Service can cause real, immediate production impact.

Because of this real world cost and blast radius, changes to LoadBalancer Service manifests deserve the same careful review as changes to a Deployment's replica count, not a casual edit made without a second look.

blocks.title: Operational Note
blocks.content: Treat every LoadBalancer Service as a billed, production critical resource, not a free convenience. A small number of well placed LoadBalancers fronting an Ingress is usually more cost effective than one per component.
Best Practices for LoadBalancer Services

Reserve LoadBalancer for the small number of Services that genuinely need a dedicated external entry point, and prefer Ingress for consolidating multiple externally facing applications behind fewer load balancers.

Use cloud provider specific annotations deliberately, to configure things like load balancer type, internal versus external visibility, and health check behavior, rather than accepting undocumented defaults silently.
Monitor the cost of every LoadBalancer Service explicitly, since an unused or forgotten one continues to be billed indefinitely until someone notices and deletes it.
Treat deletion of a LoadBalancer Service manifest with the same caution as deleting a Deployment, since it has real, immediate, external facing consequences the moment it is removed.

blocks.content: The Single Most Valuable Takeaway

LoadBalancer is the cloud native, fully automated way to give an application a genuine, stable, public entry point, and it works by layering a real external load balancer on top of the NodePort and ClusterIP machinery already established.

Its convenience should never obscure its real cost, both financial and operational, which is exactly why it should be reserved for the small number of Services that genuinely need dedicated external exposure.
The next topic, ExternalName, is a fundamentally different kind of Service, one that involves no load balancing or proxying at all, instead simply mapping a name to an external DNS record.

Keep the three layer stack in mind one more time: ClusterIP for internal routing, NodePort for a static external door, LoadBalancer for a genuinely production grade external entry point built automatically on top of both.

Before moving on, it is worth restating why this layering matters practically: a problem observed at the LoadBalancer level can almost always be narrowed down by checking the exact same NodePort and ClusterIP diagnostics already covered in earlier topics.

This is the real, lasting benefit of understanding Services as one connected system rather than five isolated types. Debugging skill built on one layer transfers directly and immediately to every layer built on top of it.
Carry that transferable debugging instinct forward into the remaining Service types still ahead in this module, and into every other Kubernetes networking topic covered later in this course.

blocks.title: LoadBalancer In Full
points: LoadBalancer Services instruct the cloud controller manager to automatically provision a real, external cloud load balancer for the application.
It is built directly on top of NodePort and ClusterIP; deleting either underlying layer is never necessary, since LoadBalancer manages the full stack together.
Every LoadBalancer Service is a real, billed cloud resource; avoid creating one per microservice when an Ingress controller can consolidate exposure instead.
Behavior and available annotations differ by cloud provider; on bare metal or fully on premises clusters, a tool like MetalLB is required to fill the gap.
ExternalName, covered next, is a fundamentally different kind of Service involving no load balancing at all.
